--- title: "Session 4 — Data Integration" subtitle: "Five ways to combine sources · concat · merge · the four join types · what goes wrong" --- ::: {.callout-note} **This chapter is about combining data that arrives in more than one piece.** **Assumed knowledge:** Sessions 2 and 3 — loading a DataFrame, filtering, and cleaning text columns. The text-cleaning part matters here: **you cannot join on a key you have not cleaned.** **The one idea to take away:** every join can silently lose rows or silently multiply them. **Print the row count before and after. Every time.** ::: ## 🎯 Learning outcomes {#sec-s04-outcomes} By the end of this chapter you can: 1. Describe the five approaches to data integration and pick one for a situation. 2. Stack tables with `concat` and link tables with `merge`. 3. Use all four join types and predict how many rows each returns. 4. Detect a join that lost rows and a join that multiplied them. 5. Fix the three things that break a join: mismatched keys, different names for the same thing, and duplicate keys. ## How this chapter is organised {#sec-s04-organisation} | Part | Question it answers | |---|---| | [A — Five ways to integrate](#sec-s04-a) | *Why is data split up, and what are the options for putting it together?* | | [B — Doing it in pandas](#sec-s04-b) | *How do I actually link two tables?* | | [C — What goes wrong](#sec-s04-c) | *Why did my row count change, and which of my rows disappeared?* | # Part A — Five ways to integrate {#sec-s04-a} ## 1. Why data is never in one place {#sec-s04-topic-1} **Data integration is combining data from several sources into one view you can analyse.** It exists because organisations do not store data for the convenience of analysts. Sales sit in the sales system, support tickets in the helpdesk, web visits in the analytics tool. Each was built for its own job. **The question "do customers who contact support buy less?" touches all three, and no single system can answer it.** ::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Analogy — the wedding guest list"} One partner keeps family names in a notebook; the other keeps friends in a spreadsheet. Neither list is wrong. But you cannot count chairs, order food or print place cards until they are one list. **The painful part is not the copying — it is that "R. Sharma" and "Raj Sharma" might be the same person, or might be two people.** That question is the whole of data integration. ::: ## 2. The five approaches {#sec-s04-topic-2} **There are five ways to combine sources. They differ in one thing: how much data you copy, and who does the translating.** | Approach | What happens | Data is copied? | Good | Bad | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Physical** (data warehouse) | copy everything into one central database on a schedule | **yes** | fast queries; one place to look | data is as old as the last copy; expensive | | **Virtual** (federation) | leave data where it is; a layer queries each source live when asked | **no** | always current; nothing to store | slow; breaks when any source is down | | **Application-based** | each application translates and pushes its own data to the others | partly | no central system needed | every app must know about every other; *n* apps means many links | | **Middleware** | one translation layer sits between sources and converts formats | partly | apps stay simple; one place to fix | the middleware becomes a single point of failure | | **Manual** | a person exports CSVs and combines them by hand | yes | needs nothing; works today | slow, unrepeatable, **and error-prone** | ### How to choose ```{mermaid} flowchart TD Q1{"Does the answer have to be
up to the second?"} Q1 -- yes --> V["Virtual
query the sources live"] Q1 -- no --> Q2{"Will the same question
be asked repeatedly?"} Q2 -- no --> M["Manual
a one-off export is fine"] Q2 -- yes --> Q3{"Many systems that must
talk to each other?"} Q3 -- yes --> MW["Middleware
one translation layer"] Q3 -- no --> P["Physical
copy into a warehouse"] ``` ::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Manual integration is where most reporting errors come from"} Copying and pasting between spreadsheets leaves no record of what was done, cannot be repeated identically, and fails silently when a column shifts by one. **If a manual integration is going to happen more than twice, write the code instead.** ::: # Part B — Doing it in pandas {#sec-s04-b} ## 3. Stacking versus linking {#sec-s04-topic-3} **There are two different operations, and mixing them up is the most common beginner error.** | Operation | Question it answers | Function | |---|---|---| | **Stacking** | "here are more rows of the same thing" | `pd.concat` | | **Linking** | "here is extra information about the same things" | `pd.merge` | Two months of sales → **stack**. Customers and their orders → **link**. ```{mermaid} flowchart LR subgraph S["concat — stacking"] A1["Jan sales
100 rows"] --> C1["200 rows
same columns"] A2["Feb sales
100 rows"] --> C1 end subgraph M["merge — linking"] B1["customers
name, city"] --> C2["one row per match
more columns"] B2["orders
amount, date"] --> C2 end ``` ### Demo 1 — stacking with concat ::: {#989246f1 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd jan = pd.read_csv("datasets/sales_jan.csv") feb = pd.read_csv("datasets/sales_feb.csv") print("January:"); print(jan) print("\nFebruary:"); print(feb) print() stacked = pd.concat([jan, feb], ignore_index=True) print(stacked) print(f"\n{len(jan)} + {len(feb)} = {len(stacked)} rows. Columns unchanged: {list(stacked.columns)}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` January: date amount 0 2024-01-05 250 1 2024-01-19 90 February: date amount 0 2024-02-02 410 1 2024-02-27 130 date amount 0 2024-01-05 250 1 2024-01-19 90 2 2024-02-02 410 3 2024-02-27 130 2 + 2 = 4 rows. Columns unchanged: ['date', 'amount'] ``` ::: ::: `ignore_index=True` renumbers the rows. Without it you get row labels 0, 1, 0, 1 — two rows labelled 0, which causes confusing errors later. ::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ concat lines columns up by *name*"} If one month's file calls the column `amount` and the other calls it `Amount`, `concat` does not complain. It creates **both** columns and fills each with blanks where the other was used. **Check `.columns` on both tables before stacking.** ::: ::: {#d975921e .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} mismatched = pd.read_csv("datasets/sales_mar.csv") # this file spells it "Amount" print("March, as it arrived:"); print(mismatched) oops = pd.concat([jan, mismatched], ignore_index=True) print() print(oops) print("\nTwo amount columns, both half empty — and no error was raised.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` March, as it arrived: date Amount 0 2024-03-01 500 date amount Amount 0 2024-01-05 250.0 NaN 1 2024-01-19 90.0 NaN 2 2024-03-01 NaN 500.0 Two amount columns, both half empty — and no error was raised. ``` ::: ::: ## 4. Linking tables with merge {#sec-s04-topic-4} **`merge` joins two tables using a shared column called the key.** The key is usually an ID. ### Demo 2 — a first merge ::: {#80fa94a3 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd customers = pd.read_csv("datasets/customers.csv") purchases = pd.read_csv("datasets/purchases.csv") print("customers:"); print(customers) print("\npurchases:"); print(purchases) joined = pd.merge(customers, purchases, on="user_id", how="inner") print("\nInner join:"); print(joined) print(f"\ncustomers {len(customers)} rows + purchases {len(purchases)} rows → {len(joined)} rows") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` customers: user_id name city 0 1 Alice Mumbai 1 2 Bob Delhi 2 3 Chan Mumbai 3 4 Devi Pune purchases: purchase_id user_id amount 0 101 1 250.0 1 102 1 120.0 2 103 3 75.5 3 104 5 300.0 Inner join: user_id name city purchase_id amount 0 1 Alice Mumbai 101 250.0 1 1 Alice Mumbai 102 120.0 2 3 Chan Mumbai 103 75.5 customers 4 rows + purchases 4 rows → 3 rows ``` ::: ::: Read that row count carefully. **Four and four made three.** Bob and Devi vanished (no purchases), user 5 vanished (not a known customer), and Alice appears twice (two purchases). This is normal, and it is why you check. ## 5. The four join types {#sec-s04-topic-5} **The join type answers one question: which rows do you keep when there is no match?** | Type | Keeps | Use when | |---|---|---| | `inner` | only rows matching in **both** | you need complete records | | `left` | **all** left rows; blanks where no match | the left table is your population | | `right` | **all** right rows | rare — usually a `left` with the tables swapped | | `outer` | **everything** from both | you are looking for what does not match | ### Demo 3 — all four, on the same two tables ::: {#767a765e .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} for how in ["inner", "left", "right", "outer"]: result = pd.merge(customers, purchases, on="user_id", how=how) names = result["name"].fillna("(unknown)").tolist() print(f"{how:>6}: {len(result)} rows — {names}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` inner: 3 rows — ['Alice', 'Alice', 'Chan'] left: 5 rows — ['Alice', 'Alice', 'Bob', 'Chan', 'Devi'] right: 4 rows — ['Alice', 'Alice', 'Chan', '(unknown)'] outer: 6 rows — ['Alice', 'Alice', 'Bob', 'Chan', 'Devi', '(unknown)'] ``` ::: ::: Now read what each one is *for*: ::: {#10328b56 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} print("LEFT — every customer, whether or not they bought anything:") left = pd.merge(customers, purchases, on="user_id", how="left") print(left[["name", "city", "amount"]]) print("\nWho has never bought anything? The rows where amount is blank:") print(left[left["amount"].isna()]["name"].tolist()) print("\nOUTER — everything, including the purchase by an unknown user 5:") outer = pd.merge(customers, purchases, on="user_id", how="outer") print(outer[outer["name"].isna()][["user_id", "purchase_id", "amount"]]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` LEFT — every customer, whether or not they bought anything: name city amount 0 Alice Mumbai 250.0 1 Alice Mumbai 120.0 2 Bob Delhi NaN 3 Chan Mumbai 75.5 4 Devi Pune NaN Who has never bought anything? The rows where amount is blank: ['Bob', 'Devi'] OUTER — everything, including the purchase by an unknown user 5: user_id purchase_id amount 5 5 104.0 300.0 ``` ::: ::: **The `left` join answered a business question the `inner` join could not**: which customers have never purchased. An inner join deletes exactly those people. ::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Analogy — the class register"} `inner` — students who are on the register **and** sat the exam. `left` — the whole register; those who missed the exam show a blank mark. `outer` — the register plus any exam papers from people who are not on it. **The blanks are not a nuisance. They are usually the finding.** ::: ## 6. Aggregate, then join {#sec-s04-topic-6} **When one side has many rows per key, joining directly multiplies rows. Usually you want a summary instead.** ### Demo 4 — one row per customer ::: {#69c442b8 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Wrong for most purposes: Alice appears twice, so any count of customers is now wrong. naive = pd.merge(customers, purchases, on="user_id", how="left") print(f"Naive join: {len(naive)} rows for {len(customers)} customers") # Right: summarise the many side first, then join one-to-one. per_customer = purchases.groupby("user_id").agg( n_purchases=("purchase_id", "count"), total_spent=("amount", "sum"), ).reset_index() summary = pd.merge(customers, per_customer, on="user_id", how="left") summary["n_purchases"] = summary["n_purchases"].fillna(0).astype(int) summary["total_spent"] = summary["total_spent"].fillna(0) print(f"\nAggregate-then-join: {len(summary)} rows for {len(customers)} customers") print(summary) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Naive join: 5 rows for 4 customers Aggregate-then-join: 4 rows for 4 customers user_id name city n_purchases total_spent 0 1 Alice Mumbai 2 370.0 1 2 Bob Delhi 0 0.0 2 3 Chan Mumbai 1 75.5 3 4 Devi Pune 0 0.0 ``` ::: ::: **One row per customer, every customer present, spending totalled.** This aggregate-then-join pattern is the one you will use most often in real work. # Part C — What goes wrong {#sec-s04-c} ## 7. The three failures {#sec-s04-topic-7} ### Failure 1 — the key does not match **The most common cause of "the join returned nothing".** The keys look identical to a human and differ to a computer. ::: {#c2dabe68 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} left_tbl = pd.read_csv("datasets/subscribers_plan.csv") right_tbl = pd.read_csv("datasets/subscribers_spend.csv") print("The two files, side by side — the emails LOOK identical:") print(left_tbl.to_dict("records")) print(right_tbl.to_dict("records")) print("\nJoining as-is:") print(pd.merge(left_tbl, right_tbl, on="email", how="inner")) print("→ 0 rows. One key has capitals, the other has a trailing space.\n") for t in (left_tbl, right_tbl): t["email"] = t["email"].str.strip().str.lower() print("After cleaning the key:") print(pd.merge(left_tbl, right_tbl, on="email", how="inner")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` The two files, side by side — the emails LOOK identical: [{'email': 'ASHA@mail.com', 'plan': 'gold'}, {'email': 'brij@mail.com ', 'plan': 'silver'}] [{'email': 'asha@mail.com', 'spend': 900}, {'email': 'brij@mail.com', 'spend': 400}] Joining as-is: Empty DataFrame Columns: [email, plan, spend] Index: [] → 0 rows. One key has capitals, the other has a trailing space. After cleaning the key: email plan spend 0 asha@mail.com gold 900 1 brij@mail.com silver 400 ``` ::: ::: **Clean the key before you join.** Trim spaces, fix the case, standardise the format. This is why Session 3 comes before this chapter. ### Failure 2 — the same thing, different column names ::: {#b6f842bf .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} orders = pd.read_csv("datasets/orders_by_ref.csv") # this file calls the key cust_ref merged = pd.merge(customers, orders, left_on="user_id", right_on="cust_ref", how="inner") print(merged[["user_id", "name", "cust_ref", "total"]]) print("\n`left_on` and `right_on` join columns that mean the same thing but are named differently.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` user_id name cust_ref total 0 1 Alice 1 500 1 2 Bob 2 250 `left_on` and `right_on` join columns that mean the same thing but are named differently. ``` ::: ::: ### Failure 3 — duplicate keys multiply rows **This is the dangerous one, because nothing fails.** The code runs, the model trains, the numbers look plausible, and they are wrong. ::: {#cae63bd5 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} # A dirty reference table: 'Mumbai' is listed twice by mistake. regions = pd.read_csv("datasets/regions_dirty.csv") print(regions) print() blown_up = pd.merge(customers, regions, on="city", how="left") print(f"customers: {len(customers)} rows → after joining regions: {len(blown_up)} rows") print(blown_up[["user_id", "name", "city", "region"]]) print("\nAlice and Chan each appear twice. Every total computed from this table is now") print("double-counted for Mumbai — and nothing raised an error.") # The fix: make sure the lookup table has one row per key before joining. regions_clean = regions.drop_duplicates(subset="city") fixed = pd.merge(customers, regions_clean, on="city", how="left") print(f"\nAfter de-duplicating the lookup table: {len(fixed)} rows") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` city region 0 Mumbai West 1 Delhi North 2 Pune West 3 Mumbai West customers: 4 rows → after joining regions: 6 rows user_id name city region 0 1 Alice Mumbai West 1 1 Alice Mumbai West 2 2 Bob Delhi North 3 3 Chan Mumbai West 4 3 Chan Mumbai West 5 4 Devi Pune West Alice and Chan each appear twice. Every total computed from this table is now double-counted for Mumbai — and nothing raised an error. After de-duplicating the lookup table: 4 rows ``` ::: ::: ## 8. The check that catches all three {#sec-s04-topic-8} **One helper function, used after every join, catches every failure in this chapter.** ::: {#6000adc1 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} def check_join(left, right, result, name="join"): """Report what a join did to the row count, and whether keys went unmatched.""" print(f"{name}: left {len(left)} × right {len(right)} → result {len(result)}") if len(result) > len(left): print(f" ⚠ GREW by {len(result)-len(left)} rows — the right table has duplicate keys") elif len(result) < len(left): print(f" ⚠ SHRANK by {len(left)-len(result)} rows — some left keys had no match") else: print(" ✓ one row in, one row out") blanks = result.isna().sum() if blanks.any(): print(f" unmatched values appear as blanks in: {blanks[blanks>0].to_dict()}") check_join(customers, regions, blown_up, "customers + dirty regions") print() check_join(customers, regions_clean, fixed, "customers + clean regions") print() check_join(customers, purchases, pd.merge(customers, purchases, on="user_id"), "customers + purchases (inner)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` customers + dirty regions: left 4 × right 4 → result 6 ⚠ GREW by 2 rows — the right table has duplicate keys customers + clean regions: left 4 × right 3 → result 4 ✓ one row in, one row out customers + purchases (inner): left 4 × right 4 → result 3 ⚠ SHRANK by 1 rows — some left keys had no match ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ A join that changes the row count is a claim, not an accident"} A shrinking join says *"these records had no match"*. A growing join says *"one of these keys is not unique"*. Both may be fine — but **you should be able to say which, and why**, before you use the result. ::: # 🎯 Tasks {#sec-s04-tasks} ::: {.callout-note title="✏️ Practise"} **Task 1 — Predict, then check.** Before running anything, write down how many rows each of the four join types will return for `customers` and `purchases`. Then run Demo 3. **Report which you got wrong and why.** **Task 2 — Find the silent customers.** Using a left join, list every customer who has never made a purchase. **Task 3 — Break it, then fix it.** Add a second `"Delhi"` row to the `regions` table. Join, and use `check_join` to detect the damage. Then fix it. **Task 4 — Aggregate then join.** Produce a table with one row per **city** showing the number of customers and the total amount spent by customers in that city. ::: :::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"} ::: {#a4906a33 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd customers = pd.read_csv("datasets/customers.csv") purchases = pd.read_csv("datasets/purchases.csv") # Task 1 — inner 3, left 5, right 4, outer 6 for how in ["inner","left","right","outer"]: print(f"Task 1 — {how:>6}: {len(pd.merge(customers, purchases, on='user_id', how=how))} rows") # Task 2 left = pd.merge(customers, purchases, on="user_id", how="left") print("\nTask 2 — never purchased:", left[left["amount"].isna()]["name"].tolist()) # Task 4 — aggregate the many side, then join, then group by city per_cust = purchases.groupby("user_id")["amount"].sum().reset_index(name="spent") by_city = (pd.merge(customers, per_cust, on="user_id", how="left") .assign(spent=lambda d: d["spent"].fillna(0)) .groupby("city") .agg(customers=("user_id","count"), total_spent=("spent","sum"))) print("\nTask 4:"); print(by_city) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Task 1 — inner: 3 rows Task 1 — left: 5 rows Task 1 — right: 4 rows Task 1 — outer: 6 rows Task 2 — never purchased: ['Bob', 'Devi'] Task 4: customers total_spent city Delhi 1 0.0 Mumbai 2 445.5 Pune 1 0.0 ``` ::: ::: :::: # ❓ MCQs {#sec-s04-mcqs} **Q1.** A dashboard must show live warehouse stock, and stock changes every few seconds. Which approach? - (a) Physical integration into a nightly warehouse. - (b) **Virtual integration, querying the stock system directly.** - (c) Manual integration. **Q2.** Twelve internal systems each need data from the other eleven, and every team is writing its own converter. Which approach fixes this? - (a) Manual integration. - (b) Virtual integration. - (c) **Middleware — one translation layer instead of many pairwise converters.** **Q3.** You have 1,000 customers and join a `city → region` lookup. You get 1,043 rows. What happened? - (a) 43 customers were added. - (b) **The lookup table has duplicate city entries, so some customers matched twice.** - (c) The join type was wrong. **Q4.** You want every product listed in a sales report, including those that sold nothing this month. Which join? - (a) `inner`, from sales to products. - (b) **`left`, from products to sales.** - (c) `right`, from products to sales. **Q5.** A merge on `email` returns 0 rows even though both tables clearly contain the same people. Most likely cause? - (a) Pandas is broken. - (b) **The keys differ in case or whitespace.** - (c) The tables are too large. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answers"} **A1 — (b).** A nightly copy would show yesterday's stock, which for this question is worse than useless. Virtual integration trades speed for freshness, and freshness is what this dashboard is for. **A2 — (c).** With 12 systems talking directly, you can end up maintaining dozens of converters. Middleware means each system talks to one thing. **A3 — (b).** Demo in Failure 3. Every total computed afterwards is inflated for the duplicated cities. **A4 — (b).** Start from the table whose rows you want to keep all of. Products with no sales come through with blank sales figures — which is exactly the answer you wanted. **A5 — (b).** Failure 1. `"ASHA@mail.com"` and `"asha@mail.com"` are different strings. ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="✅ Before you move on"} - [ ] I can name all five integration approaches and choose between them - [ ] I know when to `concat` and when to `merge` - [ ] I can predict the row count of an inner, left, right and outer join - [ ] I clean the key column before joining on it - [ ] **Easiest thing to forget:** check the row count after every join. A join that quietly doubles rows produces totals that are wrong and never raises an error. :::
